The force is gradually increased to a maximum at Q and then gradually decreased to zero at R.
Which statement is correct?
A
Along the line PQ, the wire obeys Hooke’s law.
B
Along the line RP, the spring constant is equal to
.
force
extension
C
The wire has elastic deformation at point Q.
D
The work done in stretching the wire to P is equal to (force  extension) at point P.

hints: Notice the axes: extension is on the vertical axis and force on the horizontal axis, with loading O to Q via P and unloading Q back to R at the origin.
Recall Hooke's law needs a straight line through the origin for $F = kx$, and spring constant $k$ is force divided by extension, not the inverse.
Check whether any permanent extension remains when force returns to zero at R to decide if deformation to Q was elastic or plastic.
walkthrough: Identify the paths: increasing force follows 0-P-Q and decreasing force follows Q to R, where R is at zero force and zero extension.
Test Hooke's law: it requires $extension \propto force$, a straight line through the origin on this plot. The loading curve bends near PQ, so proportionality is lost.
Test work done: work is area under force against extension, giving $W = \frac{1}{2}Fx$ for a linear section, not $F \times x$.
Test elasticity: elastic deformation means the wire returns to its original length when load is removed. Here the unloading curve finishes at R at the origin, so extension is zero when force is zero.
Therefore there is no residual extension and deformation at Q was still elastic. This is option C

A.explanation: PQ is curved on this extension against force plot, so extension is not proportional to force there and Hooke's law $F = kx$ is not obeyed.

B.explanation: Spring constant is $k = \text{force} / \text{extension}$, not extension divided by force, and RP is a curved unloading path not a single gradient.

C.explanation: The unloading curve returns to zero extension at zero force at R, so there is no permanent extension and deformation up to Q is elastic.

D.explanation: Work done is the area under a force against extension graph, which to P is $\frac{1}{2}Fx$ for the straight section, not $F \times x$.
